item.title: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
item.description:
Amazon has hundreds of satellites in storage waiting for rides to space.

A European Ariane 6 launcher propelled 36 satellites into orbit for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation Tuesday, continuing the network’s build-out after 40 satellites were lost earlier this month during afailure of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket.

The launch was an important rebound for Amazon, bringing the Amazon Leo fleet to 432 satellites as the company seeks to fill the void left by the grounding of ULA’s Vulcan rocket, Amazon’s primary launch provider. Now, an Amazon official tells Ars it is accelerating several Falcon 9 launches the company has purchased from SpaceX, which also owns the Starlink satellite network that Amazon seeks to dethrone.

The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo is now planned for December, Amazon said, moved forward from its previous launch date next year. Several more Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites in rapid succession after the December flight.

Amazon cast a wide net when it started signing deals for launch services five years ago, securing rides on 108 flights with every available medium- or heavy-lift rocket in the West to place a fleet of 3,232 satellites into low-Earth orbit. As of Tuesday, Amazon and its launch partners have completed 17 of those flights, with one mission failure.

Amazon executives initially bought up capacity from US-based United Launch Alliance, Europe’s Arianespace, and Blue Origin. Nearly all of those launch contracts depended on rockets still in development: ULA’s Vulcan, Europe’s Ariane 6, and Blue Origin’s New Glenn.

Each launch vehicle faced development delays, as all new rockets do. New Glenn has been grounded since May after an explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in Florida. ULA’s Vulcan will be sidelined for months after misfiring during a mission with Amazon satellites on November 15.

Amazon started booking launches in 2023 with SpaceX. Falcon 9 successfully launched Amazon’s first three missions last year, each with 24 satellites. Amazon soon reserved 10 more flights on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket as delays mounted with Amazon Leo’s other launch providers, especially ULA and Blue Origin.

The relationship between Amazon and SpaceX is a peculiar one. Amazon aims to catch up to SpaceX’s Starlink network, now boasting more than 11,000 satellites, to bring competition to the satellite broadband market. Federal regulators approved Amazon Leo’s second-generation constellation earlier this year, an addition that will bring the fleet to more than 7,000 satellites in the 2030s. Amazon also plans a direct-to-device service, joining SpaceX and others in the pursuit of consumer demand for mobile connectivity.

But Starlink is far ahead. SpaceX has repurposed the Starlink satellite design for use on several US military programs, and Starlink launches on Falcon 9 are winding down as SpaceX’sStarship enters service. Starship is capable of launching heavier, more powerful Starlink satellites, a culmination that will only widen the gap with Amazon and other competitors in the satellite Internet business.

Starlink’s move to Starship opens up launch slots on Falcon 9, allowing Amazon to accelerate its launches with SpaceX in the near term. But SpaceX doesn’t plan to keep Falcon 9 around for long. The company has reportedly stopped accepting commercial Falcon 9 bookings after 2028.

That means Amazon Leo needs its other launch providers to step up. Arianespace is doing so, withfour successful Ariane 6 flightsfor Amazon this year. Amazon reserved six additional flights with Arianespace in September as Ariane 6 proved its mettle.

But there are questions about Europe’s ability to ramp up production of Ariane 6 rockets, which are single-use and not reusable like Falcon 9 and New Glenn. Europe’s rocket factories are sized to support a launch cadence of up to nine or 10 Ariane 6 flights per year. Arianespace will likely reach six Ariane 6 flights this year, with one more remaining before the end of December.

European taxpayers paid for development of the Ariane 6 and the industrial capacity to build the rockets, and they continue to subsidize each Ariane 6 flight, whether it carries a European government payload or commercial satellites for a large American corporation like Amazon.

European government ministers are mulling proposals to increase Ariane 6 production to meet surging demand from commercial users and Europe’s internal space programs. A decisioncould come next month, but a ramp-up in launch cadence won’t happen overnight.

Amazon paid United Launch Alliance hundreds of millions of dollars for expansion at Cape Canaveral, Florida, to prepare for as many as 25 Vulcan launches per year. Such a launch cadence is a long way off for ULA, which has now launched Vulcan five times (with one failure) in its three years of service.

Blue Origin, owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, could resume New Glenn flights early next year after completing a launch pad rebuild. It is not clear when Amazon might begin launching on New Glenn, but finding slots in the rocket’s launch schedule could be difficult as Blue Origin prioritizes work for NASA’s Artemis lunar program.

In the meantime, SpaceX will offer Amazon its most assured rides to space. Falcon 9s can launch from Cape Canaveral every few days, and Amazon is ready to tap into that capability withhundreds of satellites in storagewaiting to go to orbit.

item.title: Amazon drone crashes on garage after delivering shampoo, draws FAA probe
item.description:
Amazon says Prime Air drones made “hundreds of thousands” of deliveries in 2026.

An Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States.

The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according toWXYZ 7 News Detroit. After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines.

“Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7.

Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-poweredMK30 dronesthat can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case—so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.

The FAApreliminary accident and incident notificationbriefly describes the incident as “UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff.” That notice was posted on November 23.

The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe,according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents.

Logan Coomes, the neighbor whose garage was struck by the drone, described an Amazon Prime Air team arriving within 10 minutes and coordinating with Detroit Edison workers to eventually remove the drone by early evening, in an interview with WXYZ 7.

The Amazon Prime Air team also reportedly told Coomes that the company would help with repairs to his garage roof, and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card on the spot. Amazon claimed that this was the first such delivery drone crash from its operations near Detroit.

However, this would also add to the handful of Amazon drone incidents already under investigation by the US government. In October 2025, two Amazon delivery dronescrashed into a construction cranein Tolleson, Arizona, while another delivery dronedowned an Internet cablein Waco, Texas, the following month.

The FAA has also been investigating an Amazon Prime Air drone crashinvolving an apartment buildingin Richardson, Texas, that occurred in February 2026.

In response to the latest crash in Michigan, an Amazon spokesperson described Prime Air drones as making nearly 6,000 flights per day and already having delivered “hundreds of thousands of packages this year” in astatement shared with CNN.

Amazon has been growing its Prime Air service with the goal of having delivery dronesreach nearly 500 cities and townsacross the United States by the end of 2026. The company has described delivery drones as enabling faster deliveries through potentially lower-emission and lower-cost operations compared with relying solely on ground vehicles.

But the growth of delivery drone services has also drawn noise complaints from people living in neighborhoods where drones operate. As Sean Gallagher has written for Ars, theconstant buzz of drones could even trigger post-traumatic stress disorderor other anxiety-related disorders—especially for people who have directly or indirectly experienced some aspect of modern drone warfare.

item.title: Measles death toll rises to 14 as national case tally nears 6,000
item.description:
Wisconsin reports 3rd measles death today; Pennsylvania reported its 9th yesterday.

Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

On November 23, Pennsylvania’s health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported itsthird measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state,an infantanda child. New York has also reported adeath, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death ofa young child between the age of 0 and 4.

The virus isn’t slowing down. Measles is the most contagious virus known; it can linger in airspace for up to two hours. Up to 90 percent of people who are not immune will fall ill after an exposure. People are considered immune if they’ve been vaccinated or been infected previously. With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, the number of susceptible people is only growing.

To keep measles from getting a foothold in a community, vaccination rates need to be 95 percent or higher.According to the latest data, only 92.4 percent of US kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshold. But even in those states, there are pockets and communities that are undervaccinated.

In Pennsylvania, which has the record for the largest measles outbreak this year so far, the epidemic curve appears to be past the peak. But, Wisconsin seems to be in the thick of its outbreak. As of today,the state case count hit 920, with 88 cases reported just since November 20. The health department has tallied 418 cases since the start of the month.

In most cases, measles causes high fever, a telltale rash, cough, runny nose, and watery eyes. But some develop complications, which can be severe and even life-threatening, including pneumonia and brain swelling, which can result in intellectual disabilities and hearing loss. Inpregnant persons, measles can cause more severe illness and pregnancy complications, including premature birth, low birth weight, and congenital measles.

After an acute infection, every person infected faces a long immune recovery in which they are newly vulnerable to a slew of other diseases. The measles virus specifically infects and destroys memory immune cells, which hold molecular records of germs the immune system has previously encountered and defeated. In other words, the immunity built up over the person’s life gets wiped, a phenomenon called immune amnesia. A study in 2019 estimated that the measles virus erasesup to 73 percent of a person’s antibody repertoire, which would otherwise defend against infections and reinfections. To regain protection, people must be exposed to the germs again, either through reinfections or repeat vaccinations.

People who appear to recover are also at risk ofsubacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare but devastating condition in which the virus remains in the central nervous system, striking years later to cause a progressive, fatal neurological disease.

item.title: What’s going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
item.description:
A new AI-assisted proof seems to be solid, but we’re not sure what it tells us.

Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof ofthe Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”

The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. Hisannouncementis written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.

But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.

The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof usinga programming language named Leanthat has allowed therapid verificationthat the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.

It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.

But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.

When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.

AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.

The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.

Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage ina formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.

Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.

But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.

By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of new ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.

Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.

How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.

This is all new and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.

But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.
